records.our_prose: California's desert valleys (Imperial, Coachella) grow beefsteak on an inverted, two-window calendar driven by extreme summer heat. The main crop is set out across the cool season, December through March, to mature and set fruit before summer; a second fall crop goes out in early fall (about September) as the heat breaks and produces into the mild winter. June through August is a climatic-absolute fruit-set exclusion: complete blossom drop for every tomato type, not narrowed for beefsteak, which is at least as heat-sensitive as cherry. Confirm local frost for the winter harvest tail. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC IPM)

records.our_prose: California's interior valleys (Sacramento, San Joaquin) grow beefsteak as a single long warm season: set transplants out April into May and harvest from midsummer into fall up to first frost. UC ANR lists one April-May tomato window with no separate fall planting, so this is one continuous crop, not a spring-and-fall split. Large-fruited beefsteak sets fewer fruit through the peak-heat weeks of the valley summer (it is more heat-sensitive than cherry types), with set resuming as nights cool; the plant stays in the ground through the dip. Cages suit the valley heat. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

records.our_prose: California's North and North Coast (Monterey County north) grow beefsteak as a single cool-limited season: set transplants out in May once daytime temperatures are reliably above 70 °F, and harvest from late summer into fall. The constraint here is cool marine air, not heat, so there is no summer pause. Large-fruited beefsteak needs warm days to ripen and can be slow in the coolest coastal pockets, so choose a variety matched to your season length and give it the warmest, most sheltered exposure. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2)

The bigger day-to-day challenges are disease, bugs, and heavy rain.

records.our_prose: Aim for about 1 to 2 inches of water a week, and water deeply so it soaks well down. Beefsteak roots go quite deep, and deep watering pulls them down where they handle heat and dry spells better; quick shallow sprinkles keep roots near the surface where they dry out fast.

records.source_context: Transplants can be watered overhead, or they may be watered from the bottom. To water transplants from the bottom, simply fill a container or lid with 1 to 2 inches of water and set the transplant tray into the water reservoir. Allow the transplant tray to absorb water for 3 to 10 minutes and place the tray back under the grow lights.

records.our_prose: Keep water off the foliage: overhead irrigation creates the leaf-surface wetness Septoria leaf spot and early blight need to infect. If overhead watering is unavoidable, do it in the morning so foliage dries before nightfall. Mulch to steady soil moisture, which also limits the blossom-end rot that large-fruited types are especially prone to.
